name: Taj Mahal
shortDesc: The pinnacle of Mughal architectural symmetry, clad in flawless Makrana white marble with pietra dura lapidary inlay.
fullDesc: Commissioned by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan as a mausoleum for his favorite wife Mumtaz Mahal, the Taj Mahal stands on a raised plinth beside the Yamuna River. It integrates Persian, Islamic, and Indian architectural sensibilities into an immaculate symmetrical quadrangle (Charbagh). The central bulbous onion dome is flanked by four freestanding minarets deliberately angled outward to prevent structural collapse onto the mausoleum in earthquakes.
highlights: Flawless bilaterally symmetrical Charbagh riverfront garden layout
Central high double dome with lotus motif and gilded bronze finial
Exquisite Parchin Kari (Pietra Dura) semi-precious stone floral inlay
Four three-story freestanding minarets leaning slightly outward
keyMaterials: Makrana White Marble, Red Sandstone plinths, Jasper, Jade, Turquoise & Lapis Lazuli
architecturalElements: Bulbous Double Dome, Iwan Portals, Jali Screens, Chatris, Calligraphic Pishtaq

name: Red Fort (Lal Qila)
shortDesc: The monumental fortified red sandstone palace-citadel of Shahjahanabad, symbolizing sovereignty and imperial majesty.
fullDesc: Constructed when Shah Jahan shifted his capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad (Delhi), the Red Fort is fortified with massive red sandstone ramparts spanning over 2.4 kilometers. Within its walls lie the Diwan-i-Aam (Hall of Public Audience) with its marble canopy throne, the Diwan-i-Khas (Hall of Private Audience) where the Peacock Throne once stood, and the tranquil pavilions along the stream of paradise (Nahr-i-Bihisht).
highlights: Massive octagonal bastions and 33-meter high sandstone curtain walls
The Lahori Gate with ceremonial barbicans built during Aurangzeb's reign
Nahr-i-Bihisht (Canal of Paradise) water system cooling the royal pavilions
Diwan-i-Khas inscribed with Amir Khusrau's couplet on earthly paradise
keyMaterials: Red Sandstone, White Makrana Marble, Gilded Copper Finials, Polished Stucco
architecturalElements: Cusped Multi-Foil Arches, Bengal-Style Curved Bangladar Roofs, Chattris, Jharokhas

name: Fatehpur Sikri & Buland Darwaza
shortDesc: Akbar's ceremonial capital featuring the colossal 54-meter Buland Darwaza and syncretic red sandstone pavilions.
fullDesc: Built upon a rocky ridge south-west of Agra, Fatehpur Sikri was founded by Akbar to honor Sufi mystic Sheikh Salim Chishti. The city represents a revolutionary fusion of Hindu, Jain, and Persian architectural idioms. The Buland Darwaza ('Gate of Magnificence'), erected to commemorate Akbar's victory over Gujarat in 1573, rises 54 meters and commands the southern approach to the grand Jama Masjid.
highlights: Buland Darwaza: 54-meter triumphal entrance arch with Quranic inscriptions
Panch Mahal: Five-tiered stepped pyramid pavilion with 176 unique columns
Diwan-i-Khas: Central carved stone pillar with 36 cantilevered serpentine brackets
Tomb of Salim Chishti: Pure white marble jewel surrounded by intricate jali lattice
keyMaterials: Sikri Red Sandstone, White Marble inlays, Carved Sandstone bracketry
architecturalElements: Stepped Hypostyle Columns, Corbelled Brackets, Chhajja Overhangs, Trabeate Lintels

name: Agra Fort (Lal Qila of Agra)
shortDesc: Massive crescent-shaped brick-and-sandstone citadel housing the Jahangiri Mahal, Khas Mahal, and Musamman Burj.
fullDesc: A UNESCO World Heritage site, Agra Fort was transformed by Emperor Akbar from an earthen brick fort into an impregnable red sandstone citadel. Covering 94 acres along the Yamuna River, it exemplifies architectural evolution: Akbar's red sandstone Jahangiri Mahal showcases indigenous Rajput beam-and-bracket construction, while Shah Jahan's later white marble additions like Khas Mahal and Musamman Burj express refined Persian lyricism.
highlights: Double battlemented sandstone walls rising 70 feet with circular bastions
Musamman Burj: Octagonal marble tower where Shah Jahan gazed upon the Taj Mahal
Jahangiri Mahal: Rajput-influenced brackets, carved friezes, and courtyards
Sheesh Mahal (Glass Palace) with Syrian convex mirror mosaic ceilings
keyMaterials: Red Sandstone, White Makrana Marble, Glass Mirror Mosaics, Lapis Lazuli
architecturalElements: Machicolations, Double ramparts, Jharokha balconies, Cusped marble arches

name: Jama Masjid of Delhi (Masjid-i-Jahan Numa)
shortDesc: One of India's largest congregational mosques, resting on a high elevated red sandstone plinth with three marble domes.
fullDesc: Commissioned by Shah Jahan and inaugurated by an Imam from Bukhara, the Jama Masjid of Delhi commands the skyline of Old Delhi. Perched atop a sandstone plinth reached by sweeping grand staircases, its vast courtyard can accommodate over 25,000 worshippers. Three black-and-white striped marble bulbous domes crown the prayer hall, flanked by two towering 40-meter minarets constructed of alternating red sandstone and marble vertical bands.
highlights: Vast courtyard capable of hosting 25,000 worshippers simultaneously
Three alternating black-and-white marble onion domes
Twin 40-meter octagonal minarets with panoramic vistas of Delhi
Three monumental gateways approached by dramatic 35-step staircases
keyMaterials: Red Sandstone, White Marble, Black Marble striping, Gilded Brass finials
architecturalElements: Cusped Arches, Pishtaq, Chattris, Striped Onion Domes, High Plinth (Kursi)

name: Amer Fort & Sheesh Mahal
patron: Raja Man Singh I & Sawai Jai Singh
shortDesc: A hillside fortress-palace celebrated for yellow and pink sandstone battlements, mirror palace, and Maota Lake reflection.
fullDesc: Amer Fort rises majestically over Maota Lake in the Aravalli Hills, constructed by Raja Man Singh I, a top commander in Akbar's court. The palace exhibits a seamless blend of Hindu Rajput chivalry and Mughal opulence across four courtyards. The Sheesh Mahal (Hall of Mirrors) is world-renowned for its concave mirror work, reflecting a single candle into a constellation of stars across intricately carved plaster walls.
highlights: Sheesh Mahal: Convex Belgian glass mirror mosaics embedded in floral stuccowork
Ganesh Pol: Triumphal gateway painted with frescoes of Lord Ganesha and geometric motifs
Diwan-i-Aam: Double row of sandstone pillars with elephant-head bracket capitals
Aram Bagh: Mughal-style four-fold Charbagh garden irrigated from Maota Lake
keyMaterials: Yellow & Pink Sandstone, Marble, Convex Glass Mirrors, Fresco Pigments
architecturalElements: Jharokha screened balconies, Bangladar vaults, Rajput brackets, Plaster friezes

name: Humayun's Tomb
shortDesc: The architectural precursor to the Taj Mahal, pioneering the grand Persian Charbagh and double-dome in India.
fullDesc: Built for the second Mughal Emperor Humayun by his senior consort Empress Bega Begum, this UNESCO World Heritage monument is the first garden-tomb on the Indian subcontinent. Designed by Persian master architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, it synthesizes Persian geometric precision with indigenous Indian craftsmanship. Its 42.5-meter high white marble double-dome dominates a monumental red sandstone platform within an eight-part paradise garden (Hasht Bihisht).
highlights: First monumental garden-tomb and precursor to the Taj Mahal
Hasht Bihisht (Eight Paradises) ground plan around a central octagonal chamber
Revolutionary high double-dome design creating majestic interior proportions
Raised 7-meter high podium containing 56 cell chambers
keyMaterials: Red Sandstone, White Marble inlays, Grey quartzite core masonry
architecturalElements: High Double Dome, Pishtaq archways, Corner Chattris, Geometric water channels

name: Bibi Ka Maqbara (Dakkani Taj)
shortDesc: The 'Taj of the Deccan' built in memory of Dilras Banu Begum, featuring elegant marble stucco and Charbagh gardens.
fullDesc: Erected by Prince Azam Shah in memory of his mother Dilras Banu Begum (Rabia-ud-Daurani), Bibi Ka Maqbara bears a striking resemblance to the Taj Mahal in Agra. Positioned against the backdrop of the Sihaychal ranges, the tomb rests on an elevated square platform surrounded by four octagonal minarets. It represents the creative adaptation of Mughal imperial forms to Deccan regional resources, combining marble with lustrous polished lime plaster.
highlights: Elevated central plinth framed by four 8-sided corner minarets
Elaborately carved floral stucco relief panels imitating pietra dura
Classic Charbagh water canals with fountain jets fed by underground aqueducts
Perforated marble jali enclosure surrounding the subterranean cenotaph
keyMaterials: Makrana Marble, Basalt stone base, Polished fine lime stucco (Chunam)
architecturalElements: Bulbous dome, Multi-tiered minarets, Jali screens, Cusped arches, Chattris

name: Tomb of I'timad-ud-Daulah (Baby Taj)
shortDesc: The exquisite white marble 'Jewel Box' that transitioned Mughal building from red sandstone to delicate pietra dura.
fullDesc: Commissioned by Empress Nur Jahan for her father Mirza Ghiyas Beg (who held the title I'timad-ud-Daulah, Pillar of the State), this tomb is often hailed as a draft or jewel-box precursor of the Taj Mahal. Set within a walled garden beside the Yamuna River, it was the first Mughal structure built entirely of white marble with polychrome pietra dura inlay depicting wine flasks, cypress trees, fruit bowls, and floral bouquets.
highlights: First Mughal monument clad completely in white marble with polychrome inlay
Four attached hexagonal corner towers capped with open chattris
Intricate pierced stone lattice windows (Jalis) creating soft dappled light
Central square pavilion crowned with a curved canopy roof
keyMaterials: White Rajasthan Marble, Semi-precious stones (Carnelian, Jasper, Onyx, Topaz)
architecturalElements: Pietra Dura (Parchin Kari), Hexagonal minarets, Canopied pavilion, Jali screens

name: Akbar's Tomb at Sikandra
shortDesc: A distinctive tiered pyramid mausoleum without a central dome, entered through the monumental four-minaret South Gate.
fullDesc: Conceived and begun by Akbar himself and completed by his son Jahangir, this 119-acre walled complex at Sikandra represents a bold architectural departure from typical Mughal domes. The tomb structure is a five-tiered truncated pyramid reminiscent of Buddhist viharas, where four red sandstone tiers support a fifth open-air terrace of pure white marble. The Southern Gateway features four freestanding white marble minarets—the first such appearance in India.
highlights: Southern Gateway featuring four graceful white marble minarets
Unique 5-tiered pyramidal structure without a conventional central dome
Topmost level composed entirely of white marble with ornate calligraphic screens
Geometric Charbagh divided by stone causeways populated with deer and peacocks
keyMaterials: Deep Red Sandstone, White Marble inlays, Polychrome ceramic glazed tiles
architecturalElements: Hypostyle colonnades, Canopied kiosk chattris, Pishtaq archways, Jali panels

name: Shalimar Bagh (Farah Baksh)
shortDesc: The imperial garden of bliss on the shores of Dal Lake, boasting cascading water terraces, chinar trees, and black marble pavilions.
fullDesc: Built by Emperor Jahangir for his beloved wife Nur Jahan in 1619 and expanded by Shah Jahan, Shalimar Bagh ('Abode of Love') is the crowning jewel of Mughal terraced gardens. Fed by an ancient canal from the Arrah River, the garden cascades through three ascending terraces: the public garden, the emperor's private garden, and the Zenana. Its Black Pavilion (Diwan-i-Khas) is supported by fluted Kashmiri black marble pillars.
highlights: Three stepped ascending garden terraces connected by an axial water canal
Black Marble Pavilion supported by carved pillars surrounded by fountain basins
Chini-khanas: Wall niches behind waterfalls lit by oil lamps at night
Avenue of century-old majestic Chinar (Platanus orientalis) trees
keyMaterials: Black Kashmiri Marble, Carved Himalayan Deodar Wood, Dressed Stone Cascades
architecturalElements: Chadar water chutes, Chini-khana niches, Baradari pavilions, Terraced fountains

name: Kailasa Temple (Cave 16)
shortDesc: The world's largest monolithic rock-cut monument, excavated top-down from a single basalt cliffside.
fullDesc: A pinnacle of Indian rock-cut engineering, the Kailasa Temple was excavated downwards from a vertical basalt cliff face, removing over 200,000 tonnes of rock without mortar or structural joints. Modeled on Mount Kailasa, the abode of Lord Shiva, it contains a multi-story vimana, assembly mandapa, Nandi shrine, two life-sized elephant statues, and 30-meter high victory pillars (dhwaja-stambhas), covered with monumental bas-reliefs depicting the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
highlights: Top-down excavation removing an estimated 200,000 tonnes of volcanic basalt
32-meter tall Dravidian Vimana tower chiseled from the living bedrock
Monolithic life-sized stone elephants and free-standing victory pillars
Epic bas-relief friezes depicting Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa
keyMaterials: Live Deccan Trap Basalt Rock (Monolithic excavation)
architecturalElements: Vimana, Mandapa, Gopura, Nandi Mandapa, Dhwaja Stambha, Dravidian Kudu arches

name: Brihadisvara Temple (Peruvudaiyar Koyil)
shortDesc: The supreme masterpiece of Chola Dravidian architecture, featuring a 66-meter granite vimana crowned by an 80-tonne kumbam.
fullDesc: Built by Emperor Rajaraja I to celebrate Chola supremacy across South India and the Indian Ocean, Brihadisvara Temple is one of the tallest granite structures in human history. The towering vimana rises in 13 tapering storeys to 66 meters, crowned by an octagonal granite capstone (kumbam) weighing approximately 80 tonnes, hoisted via a 4-mile inclined earthen ramp. The sanctuary houses a colossal 3.7-meter Shiva Lingam.
highlights: World's first all-granite temple constructed entirely with interlocking joints
66-meter Vimana tower crowned by an 80-tonne single granite capstone block
Monolithic Nandi bull carved from a single granite block weighing 25 tonnes
Vibrant 11th-century Chola ceiling frescoes depicting cosmic dance postures
keyMaterials: Coarse Granitic Rock (Interlocking dry-stone construction without mortar)
architecturalElements: Dravidian Vimana, Upapitha base, Mahamandapa, Gana friezes, Yali pillars

name: Kandariya Mahadeva Temple
shortDesc: The pinnacle of Nagara temple design, featuring an undulating mountain-like shikhara with 84 miniature subsidiary spires.
fullDesc: Dedicated to Lord Shiva, the Kandariya Mahadeva Temple represents the zenith of Central Indian Nagara temple architecture. Erected on a high masonry jagati platform, its silhouette mirrors the sacred peaks of Mount Meru. Its 31-meter shikhara comprises 84 miniature subsidiary urushringa spires clustered around the central tower. Its exterior surfaces boast over 870 intricately sculpted stone figures celebrating celestial beauties (surasundaris), deities, and human passions.
highlights: Over 870 sculpted celestial beings, dancers, and tantric deities
Shekhari-style shikhara crowned with an enormous amalaka and kalasha
High adhisthana plinth creating a circumambulatory pathway (pradakshina)
Harmonious gradation of 5 ascending pyramidal roof halls leading to the sanctum
keyMaterials: Light Buff Sandstone with mortise-and-tenon interlocking joints, Granite base
architecturalElements: Nagara Shikhara, Urushringa towers, Jagati plinth, Amalaka, Kalasha, Ardhamandapa

name: Sun Temple Konark
shortDesc: A monumental 24-wheeled stone chariot of the Sun God Surya, pulled by seven galloping horses along the Bay of Bengal.
fullDesc: Conceived as a colossal celestial chariot for the Sun God Surya, the Konark Sun Temple was designed with 24 carved stone wheels—each nearly 10 feet in diameter—and hauled by seven spirited horses. The wheels function as accurate sundials, reading solar time to within minutes. Built from Khondalite and chlorite stone using iron clamping dowels, its majestic Jagamohana (assembly porch) remains an engineering triumph of eastern India.
highlights: 24 elaborately carved stone wheels functioning as precise solar astronomical dials
Seven colossal galloping horses representing the days of the week
Monumental Jagamohana porch rising over 39 meters above sea level
Exquisite chlorite stone carvings of celestial musicians and erotic dancers
keyMaterials: Khondalite Stone, Green Chlorite, Wrought Iron interlocking dowels
architecturalElements: Deula vimana, Jagamohana, Natamandapa dance pavilion, Pitha chariot platform

name: Virupaksha & Vitthala Complex
shortDesc: The monumental capital of the Vijayanagara Empire featuring the iconic Stone Chariot and musical granite pillars.
fullDesc: Sprawling across a dramatic boulder-strewn landscape along the Tungabhadra River, Hampi was the opulent capital of the Vijayanagara Empire. The Vitthala Temple complex is renowned for its world-famous Stone Chariot (Garuda shrine) and the Ranga Mandapa with 56 musical pillars that resonate with distinct acoustic frequencies when tapped. Nearby, the Virupaksha Temple features a 50-meter, 9-tier eastern gopuram that has maintained continuous worship since the 7th century.
highlights: Monolithic Stone Chariot (Garuda shrine) with turning stone axles
56 musical pillars carved from resonant granite emitting musical notes
50-meter, 9-tiered pyramidal eastern gopuram of Virupaksha Temple
Expansive pillared Kalyana Mandapa wedding halls with yali rearing lion pilasters
keyMaterials: Hard Grey Granite, Basalt, Mortared Brick Superstructures, Polished Stucco
architecturalElements: Yali Composite Pillars, Pushkarini stepwells, Rayagopuram, Stone Chariot, Mandapa

name: Meenakshi Amman Temple
shortDesc: A vibrant sacred city-temple complex with 14 towering polychrome gopurams and the famous Hall of a Thousand Pillars.
fullDesc: Heart of the ancient Pandyan capital Madurai, the Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple is a living architectural marvel covering 14 acres. Reconstructed to its current grandeur under the Nayaka rulers, the complex is dominated by 14 monumental gopurams, the tallest rising 52 meters, adorned with thousands of polychromatic stucco sculptures of gods, demons, and celestial beings. Inside, the Hall of a Thousand Pillars contains 985 exquisitely sculpted monolithic columns.
highlights: 14 monumental multi-tiered gopurams covered with thousands of polychrome stucco figures
Ayiram Kaal Mandapam (Hall of 1000 Pillars) featuring 985 carved stone pillars
Golden Lotus Tank (Potramarai Kulam) sacred reservoir reflecting the towers
Musical stone pillars in the temple corridors tuned to classical scales
keyMaterials: Granite stone foundation and pillared colonnades, Polychrome painted stucco
architecturalElements: Towering Gopurams, Prakaram concentric corridors, Mandapa hypostyle halls

name: Shore Temple of Mamallapuram
shortDesc: The oldest structural stone temple in South India, perched heroically on the Coromandel Coast overlooking the Bay of Bengal.
fullDesc: Overlooking the surf of the Bay of Bengal, the Shore Temple marks a pivotal transition in South Indian architecture from monolithic rock-cut cave shrines to freestanding structural stone masonry. Built by Pallava king Rajasimha, it houses three shrines dedicated to Lord Shiva and Lord Vishnu (Anantasayana). Its stepped pyramidal vimana stands within an enclosure wall lined with rows of seated Nandi bull sculptures, having weathered ocean spray for over 1,300 years.
highlights: Oldest freestanding structural stone temple complex in South India
Twin multi-tiered Dravidian vimana towers crowned with octagonal shikharas
Perimeter enclosure wall crowned with sculptured monolithic Nandi bulls
Direct oceanfront alignment designed to greet ancient maritime sailors
keyMaterials: Dressed Blocks of Local Granite, Interlocking Stone Masonry
architecturalElements: Pallava Vimana, Kudus (horseshoe arches), Somaskanda relief panels, Lion pilasters

name: Dilwara Temples of Mount Abu
shortDesc: Unrivaled pure white marble temple complex renowned for lace-like carved translucent domes and ceilings.
fullDesc: Perched amidst the forested heights of Mount Abu, the Dilwara Temples are world-famous for the most astonishingly delicate marble carvings ever created. Built between the 11th and 13th centuries by Solanki ministers, the complex consists of five shrines, most notably Vimal Vasahi and Luna Vasahi. The marble ceilings, pendant drops, and pillars are carved so wafer-thin that the white stone appears almost translucent, resembling filigree lace rather than heavy stone.
highlights: Translucent marble pendant drop ceilings carved with microscopic precision
Vimal Vasahi central dome with 16 Vidyadevis (goddesses of knowledge)
Luna Vasahi lotus pendant (Padma Mandapa) carved from a single marble block
52 perimeter cell shrines (devakulikas) containing tirthankara images
keyMaterials: Pure White Makrana & Ambaji Marble
architecturalElements: Maru-Gurjara Mandapa, Torana arches, Translucent pendants, Corbelled ceilings

name: Ranakpur Jain Temple (Chaturmukha)
patron: Dharna Shah & Rana Kumbha of Mewar
shortDesc: A light-filled marble forest temple sustained by 1,444 uniquely carved pillars, no two of which are identical.
fullDesc: Set in a tranquil valley of the Aravalli Range, the Ranakpur Chaturmukha Dharana Vihara is dedicated to Adinatha, the first Jain Tirthankara. Engineered by architect Deepaka on a colossal raised plinth, the three-storey temple encompasses 29 halls, 80 domes, and 1,444 intricately sculpted marble pillars. Miraculously, every single pillar features a distinct carved design, and their geometric arrangement provides unobstructed views of the sanctum from any vantage point.
highlights: Forest of 1,444 individually carved marble pillars with completely unique designs
Ingenious multi-tier lightwells illuminating inner sanctums with natural sunlight
Central four-faced (Chaturmukha) marble image of Bhagwan Adinatha
Elaborate corbelled ceilings with concentric dancing apsara figurines
keyMaterials: Light Amber and White Rajasthan Marble, Sandstone plinths
architecturalElements: Maru-Gurjara Domes, Hypostyle forest halls, Torana brackets, Shikharas

name: Sun Temple Modhera
shortDesc: An astronomical solar marvel featuring the grand stepped Surya Kund reservoir and axial Sabha Mandapa hall.
fullDesc: Constructed on the Tropic of Cancer along the banks of the Pushpavati River by King Bhima I, the Sun Temple at Modhera is oriented so that at solar equinoxes, the first rays of the dawn sun illuminated the jeweled crown of Surya in the inner sanctum. The complex comprises three axial components: the Surya Kund (a grand geometric stepped water reservoir with 108 miniature shrines), the Sabha Mandapa (an open hall of 52 intricately carved pillars), and the Guda Mandapa (sanctum).
highlights: Surya Kund: Magnificent geometric stepped water reservoir with 108 miniature shrines
Equinoctial solar alignment directing dawn rays directly onto the sanctum deity
Sabha Mandapa featuring 52 carved pillars representing weeks of the solar year
Intricate cusped torana gateways and friezes of gods, celestial nymphs, and life cycles
keyMaterials: Golden-Buff Sandstone assembled without mortar using mortise joints
architecturalElements: Torana arches, Stepped Kund tank, Maru-Gurjara pillars, Assembled mandapas

name: Somnath Temple (Prabhas Patan)
shortDesc: The eternal first Jyotirlinga shrine of Lord Shiva, standing proudly against Arabian Sea breakers on the Saurashtra coast.
fullDesc: Known as the 'Shrine Eternal', Somnath is the premier among the twelve sacred Jyotirlinga shrines of Lord Shiva, standing where the Saraswati, Hiranya, and Kapila rivers meet the Arabian Sea. Repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt through centuries of invasions, its modern Kailas Mahameru Prasada was designed by renowned temple architect Prabhashankar Sompura. The temple tower rises 155 feet, topped by a 10-tonne kalasha finial, facing an unbroken sea route to Antarctica marked by the historic Baan Stambh.
highlights: Baan Stambh (Arrow Pillar) demonstrating unbroken sea meridian to Antarctica
155-foot high majestic Kailas Mahameru shikhara with intricate Solanki relief
Positioned directly on the Arabian Sea coast enduring sea breeze and tides
Monumental Sabha Mandapa with exquisitely sculpted ceilings and pillars
keyMaterials: Reddish Sandstone, Chiseled Granitic Blocks, Gold Plated Kalasha
architecturalElements: Kailas Mahameru Shikhara, Amalaka, Baan Stambh, Mandapa, Torana arches

name: Charminar
shortDesc: The triumphant four-minaret ceremonial archway of Hyderabad, epitomizing Qutb Shahi Shia Persian urban elegance.
fullDesc: Built by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, the fifth sultan of the Qutb Shahi dynasty, to commemorate the eradication of a devastating plague and celebrate the founding of Hyderabad, Charminar ('Four Minarets') is the emblem of the Deccan. Designed by Iranian prime minister Mir Momin Astarabadi, the square structure features four colossal 20-meter pointed arches facing the cardinal directions, crowned by four 56-meter stucco-adorned minarets with double balconies and an upper-floor mosque.
highlights: Four monumental 56-meter fluted corner minarets with carved double balconies
Four grand 20-meter wide pointed arches facing the cardinal urban axes
Upper-storey mosque with 45 covered prayer spaces and vaulted ceilings
Intricate Qutb Shahi stucco floral petal motifs and ornamental balustrades
keyMaterials: Granite, Limestone, Mortar, Crushed Marble and Pulverized Egg Stucco
architecturalElements: Fluted Minarets, Four Grand Arches (Char-Suq), Stucco Jali screens, Double balconies

name: Qutub Minar & Quwwat-ul-Islam
patron: Qutb-ud-din Aibak, Iltutmish & Firoz Shah Tughlaq
shortDesc: The world's tallest brick minaret rising 72.5 meters, adorned with Arabic calligraphy and cantilevered corbelled balconies.
fullDesc: Founded by Qutb-ud-din Aibak after the defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan and expanded by Iltutmish and Firoz Shah Tughlaq, the Qutub Minar is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the triumph of the early Delhi Sultanate. Soaring 72.5 meters in five tapering storeys, its red sandstone shaft transitions from alternating angular and rounded flutings to smooth white marble upper bands. Its projecting balconies are supported by stalactite-like corbelled honeycomb brackets inscribed with verses from the Quran.
highlights: 72.5-meter tapering victory minaret with 379 spiral interior steps
Richly carved bands of Arabic calligraphic Naskh and Kufic Quranic verses
Elaborate corbelled stalactite balconies supporting each diminishing storey
Adjacent 4th-century Gupta iron pillar that has resisted rust for 1,600 years
keyMaterials: Red and Buff Sandstone, White Marble, Reclaimed stone masonry
architecturalElements: Muqarnas stalactite corbels, Fluted shafts, Ogee arches, Calligraphic bands

name: Gol Gumbaz
shortDesc: Mausoleum of Mohammed Adil Shah boasting one of the world's largest unsupported domes and the famous Whispering Gallery.
fullDesc: Gol Gumbaz ('Round Dome') is the monumental tomb of Mohammed Adil Shah, ruler of the Bijapur Sultanate. Designed by the master engineer Yaqut of Dabul, its colossal hemispherical dome spans 44 meters in external diameter without any central pillars, supported internally by interlocking eight-pointed star pendentives. The interior Whispering Gallery echoes the softest whisper up to eleven distinct times, echoing audibly across the 38-meter wide chamber.
highlights: Massive 44-meter unsupported hemispherical dome resting on intersecting squinches
World-renowned Whispering Gallery where an acoustic whisper echoes 11 times
Four 8-storey octagonal corner towers capped with miniature bulbous domes
Vast uninterrupted single-chamber floor area exceeding 1,700 square meters
keyMaterials: Dark Grey Deccan Basalt, Lime Concrete Mortar, Hydraulic Plaster
architecturalElements: Intersecting Arch Pendentives, Whispering Gallery, Octagonal Minaret Towers

name: Alai Darwaza
shortDesc: The monumental southern gateway to the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque, introducing true pointed arches and squinch domes to India.
fullDesc: Built by Sultan Alauddin Khalji in 1311, Alai Darwaza is the earliest building in India constructed strictly using true Islamic architectural principles—a true dome on squinches and true pointed horseshoe arches. Built with red sandstone and contrasting white marble bands, its walls are adorned with Arabic Naskh inscriptions and pierced stone screens (jalis). Its graceful squinches transformed the square hall into an octagon to receive the hemispherical dome.
highlights: First building in India to feature true arches and a true dome on squinches
Horseshoe-shaped pointed arches with delicate spear-head fringe ornamentation
Contrasting polychrome red sandstone and white marble surface revetment
Deeply carved bands of Naskh calligraphy and geometric arabesques
keyMaterials: Red Sandstone, White Marble inlays, Fine Lime Plaster
architecturalElements: True Horseshoe Arch, Squinch Pendentives, Pierced Jali lattice, Inscription bands

name: Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra
shortDesc: An ancient mosque celebrated for its monumental seven-arched screen wall and carved Kufic Persian calligraphy.
fullDesc: Commissioned by Qutb-ud-din Aibak on the orders of Muhammad Ghori and embellished under Iltutmish with a monumental screen wall, Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra ('Two-and-a-Half Days' Hut') is one of the oldest surviving mosques in South Asia. Designed by Persian architect Abu Bakr of Herat, its prayer hall features 124 antique pillars supporting corbelled ceilings, fronted by a monumental screen of seven corbelled pointed arches inscribed with ornate Kufic and Tughra calligraphy.
highlights: Monumental seven-arched screen wall constructed under Sultan Iltutmish
Inscriptions in rare Floriated Kufic and Tugra scripts carved by Persian calligraphers
Fluted minarets once flanking the central archway
Prayer hall supported by 124 stacked pillars with intricate stone carving
keyMaterials: Yellow Sandstone, Granite, Carved Marble panels
architecturalElements: Screen Arches (Maqsura), Corbelled cusps, Fluted Minarets, Calligraphic friezes

name: Tughlaqabad Fort & Ghiyas-ud-din's Tomb
shortDesc: A colossal fortress city with cyclopean sloping stone ramparts and the pentagonal fortified tomb of Ghiyas-ud-din.
fullDesc: Built by the founder of the Tughlaq dynasty, Ghiyas-ud-din Tughluq, the fortress of Tughlaqabad was constructed as an impenetrable defense against Mongol invasions. Its cyclopean granite ramparts slope aggressively inwards (batter), reaching heights of 10 to 15 meters with circular bastions and crenellations. Linked by an elevated causeway across an artificial lake stands Ghiyas-ud-din's pentagonal tomb, crowned by a white marble dome and steep battered walls.
highlights: Cyclopean granite sloping ramparts (batter) spanning over 6 kilometers
Fortified pentagonal tomb-island surrounded by an artificial defensive lake
Pointed spear-headed arches combined with lintels in indigenous trabeate fashion
White marble dome crowning a red sandstone battered tomb
keyMaterials: Rough-Hewn Delhi Quartzite, Red Sandstone, White Marble
architecturalElements: Battered Sloping Walls, Cyclopean Bastions, Machicolations, Causeways

name: Ibrahim Rauza
shortDesc: The 'Taj Mahal of the South', featuring paired mausoleum and mosque raised on a common terrace with acoustic stone chains.
fullDesc: Designed by master architect Malik Sandal, Ibrahim Rauza is the funerary complex of Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II and his queen Taj Sultana. Set within a walled Charbagh garden, it comprises a mausoleum and mosque facing each other across an ornamental fountain pool. Renowned for its lace-like perforated stone jalis, slender minarets, bulbous lotus-petaled dome, and hollow stone hanging chains carved from single basalt blocks.
highlights: Miraculous stone hanging chains carved out of continuous solid blocks of basalt
Perforated stone jali walls containing entire chapters of the Quran in Arabic
Interlocking flat stone ceiling constructed with secret mortar without central support
Twin facing structures creating sublime bilateral architectural symmetry
keyMaterials: Fine-Grained Basalt Stone, Polished Lime Plaster, Gold-Leaf Highlights
architecturalElements: Hanging Stone Chains, Pierced Calligraphic Jalis, Bulbous Lotus Dome, Slender Minars

name: Tomb of Shams-ud-din Iltutmish
shortDesc: Square unroofed tomb chamber celebrated for profuse calligraphic arabesques and early squinch arch experiments.
fullDesc: Built by the third ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, Shams-ud-din Iltutmish, as his final resting place, this square tomb is celebrated for its breathtaking interior stone carving. Every inch of its red sandstone interior walls is covered in delicate low-relief arabesques, geometric patterns, and Quranic verses in Kufic and Naskh scripts. In the four upper corners, early squinch arches transformed the square chamber into an octagon, which originally supported a collapsed sandstone dome.
highlights: Intricately carved interior sandstone surfaces with near-zero uncarved space
Early squinch arches marking early Islamic doming engineering in North India
Rich Quranic inscriptions in pristine Floriated Kufic, Naskh, and Tugra scripts
Central cenotaph of white marble resting on a raised plinth
keyMaterials: Red Sandstone, White Marble cenotaph, Quartzite rubble exterior
architecturalElements: Corner Squinches, Arabesque carving, Quranic calligraphic friezes, Mihrab niche

name: Bara Gumbad & Mosque
shortDesc: A monumental square portal gateway and three-domed mosque renowned for exquisite incised plaster arabesques.
fullDesc: Standing in the serene expanse of Lodhi Gardens in central Delhi, Bara Gumbad ('Big Dome') was constructed during the reign of Sikandar Lodhi. Rather than a tomb, the imposing square domed structure served as a monumental gateway to the attached Friday Mosque (Jami Masjid) and guest house (Mehman Khana). The attached three-bay mosque boasts some of the finest incised plasterwork (stucco) in Islamic architecture, with intertwining floral arabesques and Quranic calligraphic bands.
highlights: High hemispherical dome resting on an elevated square base with corner turrets
Attached Friday Mosque featuring three ribbed domes and ogee arched openings
Unrivaled incised and painted stucco medallions and Quranic inscriptions
Opposing Mehman Khana creating a balanced tripartite architectural forum
keyMaterials: Grey Quartzite masonry, Red Sandstone inlays, Finely incised lime plaster
architecturalElements: Ogee arches, Incised stucco arabesques, Corner turrets, High drum dome

name: Hauz Khas Complex & Firoz Shah's Tomb
shortDesc: An ancient royal water reservoir, L-shaped Islamic madrasa university, and garden tomb of Sultan Firoz Shah.
fullDesc: Originally excavated by Alauddin Khalji as the royal water tank (Hauz-i-Alai) to supply the second city of Delhi (Siri), the site was transformed by Firoz Shah Tughlaq into a premier medieval center of Islamic learning. An L-shaped two-storey madrasa was erected along the reservoir banks, centered upon Firoz Shah's square mausoleum. The tomb features thick battered stone walls, an octagonal squinch drum, and an unusual exterior stone balustrade (vedika) inspired by Buddhist stupas.
highlights: L-shaped two-storey collegiate madrasa halls overlooking the royal lake
Firoz Shah's tomb with painted medallions and plaster floral rosettes on its dome
Unusual exterior stone balustrade reflecting indigenous Buddhist-Hindu influence
Picturesque assembly of multi-pillared chattris and garden pavilions
keyMaterials: Delhi Quartzite, Sandstone lintels, Plaster coating with polychrome paint
architecturalElements: Battered walls, Trabeate colonnades, Squinch dome, Madrasa cloisters

name: Golconda Fort
shortDesc: The legendary diamond citadel and fortress-palace of the Qutb Shahis, featuring acoustic warning systems and colossal battlements.
fullDesc: Rising over 120 meters above the Deccan plain on a granite hill, Golconda Fort was the capital of the Qutb Shahi Sultanate and the global trading center for legendary diamonds like the Koh-i-Noor and Hope Diamond. The fort boasts an 11-kilometer outer wall with 87 semicircular bastions. It is world-renowned for its sophisticated acoustic design: a single handclap beneath the dome of the Fateh Darwaza can be clearly heard at the Bala Hissar pavilion at the highest point a kilometer away.
highlights: Ingenious acoustic transmission carrying clapping signals from base to hilltop pavilion
Fateh Darwaza ('Victory Gate') fortified with iron elephant spikes to prevent battering
Multi-tiered layered concentric fortress walls with 87 semi-circular stone bastions
Royal palace ruins, durbar hall, and water-lifting Persian wheel mechanisms
keyMaterials: Massive Granite Ashlar Blocks, Lime Mortar, Teak Timber gates with iron spikes
architecturalElements: Acoustic Dome, Machicolations, Pointed archways, Elephant-spiked gates

name: Rashtrapati Bhavan (Viceroy's House)
patron: British Raj (Viceroy Lord Hardinge & Lord Irwin)
shortDesc: The colossal 340-room presidential palace on Raisina Hill, fusing European neoclassicism with Buddhist stupa domes and Mughal chattris.
fullDesc: Designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens as the crowning centerpiece of New Delhi, Rashtrapati Bhavan (originally Viceroy's House) covers 320 acres on Raisina Hill. Spanning four storeys and 340 rooms, it is one of the largest residences of any head of state in the world. Its monumental copper dome is inspired by the Great Stupa of Sanchi, encircled by traditional Indian stone chattris, jaalis, and a continuous projecting chhajja overhang, synthesized with Greco-Roman columns in the 'Delhi Order'.
highlights: Massive copper dome modeled directly after the 3rd-century BCE Great Stupa of Sanchi
Lutyens' custom 'Delhi Order' classical columns with sculpted Indian stone bells
Mughal Garden (Amrit Udyan) designed as a geometric terraced water park
Constructed from over 1 billion red and cream Dholpur sandstone bricks
keyMaterials: Cream & Red Dholpur Sandstone, Italian & Indian Marble, Wrought Bronze, Copper
architecturalElements: Sanchi Stupa Dome, Chhajja cornices, Jali screens, Chattris, Delhi Order Columns

name: Victoria Memorial
shortDesc: Kolkata's gleaming white Makrana marble monument to Queen Victoria, surrounded by 64 acres of manicured royal gardens.
fullDesc: Conceived by Viceroy Lord Curzon as a grand memorial following Queen Victoria's death, this monumental landmark stands on the Maidan in Kolkata. Designed by Sir William Emerson, President of the Royal Institute of British Architects, it seamlessly incorporates Italian Renaissance, British Classical, and Mughal-Deccani architectural idioms. Built entirely of Makrana white marble (from the same quarries as the Taj Mahal), its 56-meter central dome is crowned by a rotating 16-foot bronze Angel of Victory.
highlights: Clad entirely in white Makrana marble quarried from Jodhpur, Rajasthan
16-foot tall, 3-tonne bronze Angel of Victory rotating with the wind atop the dome
Corner chattris and domed corner towers reflecting Mughal and Saracenic influences
Expansive 64-acre landscaped gardens featuring reflecting ponds and bronze statues
keyMaterials: White Makrana Marble, Belgian Glass, Portland Cement foundation, Bronze
architecturalElements: High Renaissance Central Dome, Mughal Chattris, Corinthian Colonnades, Squinches

name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (Victoria Terminus)
style: Victorian High Gothic Revival with Indian Accents
shortDesc: Mumbai's UNESCO World Heritage railway terminus, blending High Victorian Gothic spires with stone peacocks and lions.
fullDesc: Originally named Victoria Terminus to honor the Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria, CST is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the busiest railway station in India. Designed by Frederick William Stevens, it represents a remarkable convergence of Victorian Italianate Gothic Revival and traditional Indian palace architecture. Its commanding central octagonal ribbed dome is topped by a colossal 4-meter statue of 'Progress', surrounded by gargoyles, stained glass windows, and stone-carved peacocks and tigers.
highlights: Central ribbed octagonal masonry dome topped by a colossal statue of Progress
Richly carved stone gargoyles, lions (symbolizing Britain), and tigers (symbolizing India)
Elaborate polychrome Italian stained-glass windows illuminating the grand concourse
Interior vaulted ceilings painted with gold stars against azurite blue backdrops
keyMaterials: Malad Yellow Stone, Porbandar Sandstone, Italian Marble, Stained Glass, Cast Iron
architecturalElements: Ribbed Groin Vaults, Pointed Gothic Arches, Rose Windows, Flying Buttresses, Turrets

name: Gateway of India
shortDesc: The basalt ceremonial water-gate of Bombay, commemorating the royal visit of King George V with Gujarati Islamic arches.
fullDesc: Standing on the waterfront at Apollo Bunder overlooking the Arabian Sea, the Gateway of India was constructed to commemorate the arrival of King George V and Queen Mary in 1911—the first visit of a reigning British monarch to India. Architect George Wittet combined the Roman triumphal arch with 16th-century Gujarati Sultanate Islamic architecture, utilizing local yellow basalt stone and reinforced concrete. In 1948, the last British troops departed through this archway, marking the end of colonial rule.
highlights: 26-meter high monumental basalt triumphal arch with a central 15-meter dome
Perforated stone jali screens and architraves inspired by Ahmadabad Sultanate mosques
Historic site where the last British troops (First Battalion, Somerset Light Infantry) departed in 1948
Constructed of local yellow basalt quarried from Kharodi near Panvel
keyMaterials: Yellow Kharodi Basalt Stone, Reinforced Concrete core, Cast Iron gates
architecturalElements: Central Hemispherical Dome, Jali screens, Side Minarets, Cusped corbels

name: India Gate (All India War Memorial)
shortDesc: The 42-meter triumphal war arch at the eastern terminus of Kartavya Path, inscribed with 13,300 fallen soldiers' names.
fullDesc: Standing at the eastern end of the ceremonial Kartavya Path (formerly Rajpath) in New Delhi, India Gate is a 42-meter high triumphal arch dedicated to the 84,000 soldiers of the British Indian Army who died in the First World War and Third Anglo-Afghan War. Designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens, its design draws inspiration from the Arc de Triomphe in Paris while maintaining clean, unornamented neoclassical proportions clad in red and pale yellow Bharatpur sandstone.
highlights: 42-meter high monumental archway inscribed with names of 13,300 fallen soldiers
Amar Jawan Jyoti eternal flame burning beneath the central arch since 1971
Low shallow domed bowl atop the monument designed to be filled with burning oil on anniversaries
Harmonious two-tone red and yellow Bharatpur sandstone cladding
keyMaterials: Pale Yellow and Red Bharatpur Sandstone, Granite plinth
architecturalElements: Triumphal Arch, Shallow Urn Dome, Inscribed cornices, Stepped base

name: Mysore Palace (Amba Vilas)
shortDesc: The breathtaking three-storey stone palace of the Wadiyars, adorned with pink marble domes, durbar halls, and 97,000 lights.
fullDesc: Commissioned by the Wadiyar dynasty after the old wooden palace burned down, Amba Vilas Palace is one of India's most visited royal estates. Designed by British architect Henry Irwin, the three-storey grey granite palace synthesizes Hindu, Mughal, Rajput, and Gothic styles. It is framed by square towers capped with deep pink marble domes, an opulent Durbar Hall with stained glass ceilings, a golden howdah throne, and is illuminated on holidays by nearly 97,000 incandescent electric bulbs.
highlights: Illuminated by nearly 97,000 golden incandescent bulbs during Dasara festivities
Opulent Durbar Hall featuring sculpted cast-iron pillars imported from Glasgow
Peacock Pavilion (Kalyana Mandapa) with stained-glass peacock dome made in Scotland
Central five-storey 145-foot tower crowned with a gilded dome
keyMaterials: Fine Grey Granite, Pink Marble Domes, Cast-iron pillars from Glasgow, Teakwood
architecturalElements: Pink Marble Domes, Cusped multi-foil arches, Canopied chattris, Cast-iron vaults

name: Senate House, University of Madras
shortDesc: Robert Chisholm's foundational masterpiece of Indo-Saracenic architecture, featuring vibrant colored tile domes and Byzantine arches.
fullDesc: Overlooking Marina Beach, the Senate House of the University of Madras is widely acknowledged as the finest and most authentic specimen of Indo-Saracenic architecture in India. Designed by Robert Fellowes Chisholm, it broke away from alien European neo-classical styles to pioneer an architectural language rooted in India's climate and heritage. The building features four corner towers crowned with polychrome glazed tile domes, horseshoe Byzantine arches, and stone carvings executed by local craftsmen.
highlights: Pioneering monument that established the Indo-Saracenic movement in colonial India
Four distinctive corner towers crowned by Byzantine-Moorish colored ceramic tile domes
Grand Central Convocation Hall measuring 130 feet by 58 feet with a 54-foot ceiling
Climatic deep verandahs and stained-glass sunshades designed for tropical Madras
keyMaterials: Red Brickwork, Porbandar Stone dressings, Polychrome Ceramic Tiles, Teak Timber
architecturalElements: Moorish Horseshoe Arches, Polychrome Domes, Minaret Turrets, Sunshade Verandahs

name: Ripon Building
shortDesc: The gleaming pure white civic headquarters of Chennai Corporation, crowned by a 43-meter Westminster clock tower.
fullDesc: Named in honor of Lord Ripon, Governor-General of India and pioneer of local self-government, the Ripon Building serves as the seat of the Greater Chennai Corporation—the oldest municipal corporation in the Commonwealth outside Britain. Commissioned in 1909, it exhibits an imposing Neoclassical blend of Corinthian, Ionic, and Palladian orders. The dazzling white three-storey edifice is centered around a 43-meter central clock tower housing an antique mechanical Westminster chime clock.
highlights: 43-meter high central clock tower housing an antique mechanical chiming clock
Pure gleaming white facade combining Ionic and Corinthian classical colonnades
Seat of the Greater Chennai Corporation, founded in 1688
South Indian teakwood staircases and imported Cuddapah and Italian marble flooring
keyMaterials: Brick masonry plastered with pristine white shell lime, Teak, Cuddapah Slate
architecturalElements: Palladian Pediments, Corinthian Pilasters, Clock Tower, Arcade Colonnades

name: Mayo College
patron: Lord Mayo (Viceroy of India) & Rajput Princes
shortDesc: The 'Eton of the East' main building, carved from pure white Makrana marble in ornate Rajasthani-Saracenic splendor.
fullDesc: Founded by Lord Mayo in 1870 to educate the sons of Indian princely royalty, Mayo College in Ajmer features a breathtaking main school building designed by Major Charles Mant of the Royal Engineers. Constructed entirely of pure white Makrana marble from the quarries of Jodhpur, the facade combines classical clock tower proportions with traditional Rajasthani chattris, jharokhas, cusped arches, and stone jaalis, creating an iconic collegiate landmark.
highlights: Constructed entirely of brilliant white Makrana marble
Central clock tower flanked by multiple Rajput chattris and canopies
Ornate carved jharokha balconies and cusped multifoil arches
Vast 300-acre campus with residential boarding houses modeled after princely states
keyMaterials: Pure White Makrana Marble, Teakwood, Stained Glass
architecturalElements: Rajput Jharokha, Chattri kiosks, Clock Tower, Cusped Arches, Jali Balustrades

name: Rajabai Clock Tower, University of Mumbai
shortDesc: Mumbai's 85-meter Venetian Gothic tower modeled after London's Big Ben, adorned with 24 statues depicting Indian castes.
fullDesc: Soaring 85 meters over the Fort campus of the University of Mumbai, the Rajabai Clock Tower was designed by renowned English Gothic revivalist Sir George Gilbert Scott, modeled on London's Big Ben. Financed by broker Premchand Roychand on condition it be named after his blind mother Rajabai, the tower is built from buff-colored Kurla stone and Porbandar stone. Its eight tiers are adorned with 24 statues sculpted by students of Sir J.J. School of Art portraying Indian ethnic groups and professions.
highlights: 85-meter (280-foot) tall landmark tower modeled after Westminster's Big Ben
24 life-size statues carved by Indian craftsmen depicting regional castes and attire
Grand 16-bell carillon mechanism that historically played tunes including 'Home! Sweet Home!'
Stunning stained-glass rose windows illuminating the University Library reading hall
keyMaterials: Buff Kurla Stone, Porbandar Sandstone, Italian Stained Glass, Teak timber
architecturalElements: Lancet Windows, Venetian Tracery, Spired Pinnacles, Groin-vaulted Portico

name: National Art Gallery (Victoria Memorial Hall)
shortDesc: A magnificent red sandstone Indo-Saracenic palace in Chennai modeled directly upon Fatehpur Sikri's Buland Darwaza.
fullDesc: Built to commemorate the Diamond Jubilee of Queen Victoria and designed by government consulting architect Henry Irwin, this jewel of the Egmore Museum complex was constructed from pink-red sandstone brought from Satyavedu in Andhra Pradesh. Irwin modeled its entrance directly after Akbar's triumphal Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri. The building features an ornate central dome, cusped arches, carved stone brackets, and deep eaves that shelter art galleries from tropical sunlight.
highlights: Modeled directly after the famous Buland Darwaza of Fatehpur Sikri
Constructed from distinctive pink-red Satyavedu sandstone
Exquisite stone carvings executed by traditional temple sculptors of Kumbakonam
Intricate pierced stone jali screens and deep overhanging chhajjas
keyMaterials: Satyavedu Red Sandstone, Granite foundations, Madras Terraced roofs
architecturalElements: Buland-style Pishtaq, Cusped Arches, Chattri turrets, Jalis, Chhajja eaves
